blocks.text: 6.7.4 Case Study: Reformulating GridCap Medium

GridCap's planning team inherits a model of the medium portfolio (400 projects over ten years) from an analyst who has moved on. It is correct: it allows exactly the plans the business rules allow. It also uses two forms section 6 has called weak, the aggregated work-front row of lesson 6.7.1 and the aggregated, big-M precedence row of lesson 6.4.3. HiGHS needs 3,856 nodes to solve it to its default gap. The team's lead asks the question every inherited model raises: "Can we make this solve faster by writing it better?"

This lesson answers it the way a careful engineer would, in five rules: measure first, let the LP point show the weak rows, try each lever of this module and record what it finds, then measure the solver again, and only then decide what to keep. The answer turns out to be more interesting than "yes".
GridCap is a fictional utility's portfolio, generated for this course. The work fronts and their fees are lesson 6.7.1's own addition.
The Model

The model of lesson 6.7.1 on GridCap medium: 400 projects, 10 years, 12 work fronts, 39 must-do projects, 18 parent-child pairs and 18 alternative groups. Its two inherited rows, marked, are the weak forms; the reformulated model replaces them with the forms below them.
**Sets.** $`P`$, $`Y`$, $`T_i`$, $`M`$, $`\mathcal{G}`$, $`C`$ with $`p(c)`$ and $`L_c`$, $`F`$ and $`P_f`$, as in lesson 6.7.1.
**Parameters.** $`\text{npv}_{i,t}`$, $`c_{i,k}`$, $`B_y`$ and the fees $`\phi_f`$ ($k), as in lesson 6.7.1.
**Variables.** $`x_{i,t} \in \{0, 1\}`$ for $`i \in P`$, $`t \in T_i`$ (887 of them); $`y_f \in \{0, 1\}`$ for $`f \in F`$ (12). With $`s_i = \sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t}`$.
**Objective.**
\max \; \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i} \text{npv}_{i,t}\, x_{i,t} \;-\; \sum_{f \in F} \phi_f\, y_f
**Constraints.**
with $`M_c = \max T_{p(c)} + L_c`$, the smallest valid constant (lesson 6.4.3).
Measure Before You Reformulate: Size, LP Bound and Root Bound

A reformulation is a change made to improve a number, so the numbers come first. Lesson 6.7.1 named three that a formulation decides or strongly influences, and the audit records all three for the model as inherited and after each change, one change at a time:

items: **size:** variables and rows;
**LP bound:** the formulation's own bound, solved with GLOP;
**root bound:** HiGHS's bound after presolve and its root cuts, read with `node_limit=1`.

blocks.text:
for label, fronts, precedence in steps:
    lp = lp_bound(build(medium, integer=False, fronts=fronts, precedence=precedence).model).objective_value()
    milp = build(medium, fronts=fronts, precedence=precedence).model
    variables, rows = size(milp)
    print(f"{label:22}  {variables:9}  {rows:4}  {lp:10,.2f}  {root_bound(milp):,.0f}")

step                    variables  rows  LP bound    HiGHS root bound
inherited                     899   476  190,640.68  159,535
fronts disaggregated          899   864  159,597.31  159,536
precedence cumulative         899   869  159,597.31  159,535

The fourth number, the solver's search, is the expensive one, and it comes last (the fourth rule). The order is deliberate: each line costs seconds, and it already tells you where the formulation differs from what the solver works with.
The LP Point Shows Where a Formulation Is Weak

The inherited LP bound, $190,640.68k, is far above every other number in the table. Where does the excess come from? The LP's optimal point says so: look for variables that should be 0 or 1 and are not.
inherited LP: fronts strictly between 0 and 1: 12 of 12 (from 0.38 to 0.64); starts: 13 of 887

All twelve fronts sit between 0.38 and 0.64, while only 13 of the 887 start variables are fractional. The fractions come from the rows, not the costs: the objective only picks which allowed point is best, and only the rows decide which fractional points are allowed. That is the signature lesson 6.7.1 explained: with the aggregated row, a front mobilized at 0.5 can run up to half its projects in full while paying half its fee. The remedy is the disaggregated row, one per project, and the second line of the table shows its effect: the LP bound falls by $31,043k, to $159,597.31k.

The precedence rows are the other inherited weakness. Lesson 6.4.3 found the cumulative form never weaker, and tighter in some scenarios. On GridCap medium it changes nothing: the third line's LP bound is the second's to the cent. With five more rows. A change that does not move the bound here can still be worth keeping (its rows need no big-M, and they read as plain English), but it is not a speed-up, and the audit says so.

How much of the inherited gap did the reformulation close? The best plan is worth about $159,435k (the fourth rule's solve), so by lesson 6.7.1's measure $`(190{,}640.68 - 159{,}597.31) / (190{,}640.68 - 159{,}435) \approx 99.5\%`$. Almost the whole distance from the inherited LP bound to the best plan was the front rows.
<!-- practice 1 -->
Try Each Lever, and Record What It Finds, Even Nothing
A case study is also a checklist. The other levers of this module have nothing to do with the front rows, so each is run on the medium model as it is, and its finding is recorded:

items: **Bound tightening (lesson 6.7.2):** starts that no plan can use, from the budget rows and the must-dos' floors.
**Valid inequalities (lesson 6.7.2):** pairs of starts that no plan can use together and that no row already says, the raw material of clique rows.
**Symmetry (lesson 6.7.3):** projects identical in every number the model reads, which would make plans appear several times.

blocks.text:
starts fixable from the budget rows: 0; conflicts not already a row: 0
groups of identical projects: 0

Nothing, three times. That is a real finding, not a failed step. GridCap medium's yearly budgets are $34,000k to $43,000k against projects of at most a few thousand, so no single start and no pair of starts can overflow a year (the room argument of lesson 6.7.2 needs a project that is large next to the row); and no two of medium's projects are identical. On GridCap small with hard crew rows (lesson 6.7.2), the same code found eight fixings and 70 new conflicts, because crew limits of 2 to 34 crew-months are small next to the projects. The levers depend on the data's shape, which is why the audit runs them rather than assuming.
The Solver's Own Work Decides Whether a Reformulation Solves Faster
Now the measurement that answers the lead's question: solve both models with HiGHS, as the team would in production, to HiGHS's default relative gap of $`10^{-4}`$ (0.01%):
result = solve_highs(sm.model)          # HiGHS's default relative gap: 1e-4

model          plan value  proven bound  gap      nodes
inherited         159,434       159,449  0.0094%  3,856  OPTIMAL
reformulated      159,435       159,450  0.0094%  7,823  OPTIMAL
same plan: False; starts that differ: 14

The reformulated model did **not** solve faster. It took 7,823 nodes against the inherited model's 3,856. The audit table had already given the reason it could not be much faster: the root bounds were equal, $159,535k and $159,536k. Whatever the inherited front rows lost, HiGHS's presolve and root cuts had recovered before the first branch, exactly as lesson 6.7.1 measured on GridCap small. From there the two searches start level and go different ways, and the inherited one happened to be shorter. The counts are not noise: HiGHS's node counts repeat from run to run on the same model (the module's tests solve twice and compare), so one measurement of each is enough here.

The two plans differ in 14 starts and by $1k in value. Both runs stopped as soon as their plan was proved within 0.01% of the best possible, which is what `OPTIMAL` means under a gap tolerance (lesson 3.4.3); a gap of $15k on a portfolio of $159,000k is inside it. Since both models allow exactly the same plans, either plan is valid in either model.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Keep the Strong Form for What It Is Worth, and Say What It Is Not
So what does the team keep? The audit gives an answer with its reasons, which is what a lead can act on:

items: **Keep the disaggregated fronts.** The model's own LP bound moves from $31,206k above the best plan to $162k above it. That bound is the number the team can report without trusting a solver's internal cuts; it holds for any solver or version; and any method of section 11 that works with the LP relaxation directly (decomposition, rounding heuristics, the LP bounds of a rolling horizon) inherits it. It costs 388 rows.
**Keep the cumulative precedence**, for its readability and its lack of a big-M, and record that on this data it changes no bound.

**Do not claim a speed-up.** On this model and this solver it did not happen. A reformulation's effect on run time is measured, per solver, on the data that matters, and HiGHS's own presolve and cuts are part of what is being measured.

**Look elsewhere for speed.** The root bound sits about $100k above the best plan, and the levers of this module found nothing more to cut there: no fixings, no conflicts, no symmetry. Section 11 takes it from there, with warm starts, parameter tuning and decomposition.

blocks.text: The lesson for the next inherited model is the order of the work: measure size, LP bound and root bound; let the LP point point at weak rows; run every lever and record what it finds; measure the solve; and report the result you got, including when it is not the one you expected.
Summary

items: **Measure before you reformulate: size, LP bound and root bound.** Each costs seconds and is recorded for every step.
**The LP point shows where a formulation is weak.** All twelve fronts fractional pointed at the front rows; disaggregating them closed about 99.5% of the inherited LP gap.
**Try each lever, and record what it finds, even nothing.** No fixings, no conflicts and no identical projects on GridCap medium, because its budgets are large next to its projects.
**The solver's own work decides whether a reformulation solves faster.** Equal root bounds; 3,856 nodes inherited against 7,823 reformulated.
**Keep the strong form for what it is worth, and say what it is not.** A bound that does not depend on the solver, at a cost of 388 rows; not a speed-up here.

blocks.text: **Further reading:** [MathOpt `SolveParameters`](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/python/parameters.py) (OR-Tools source): `node_limit`, `presolve`, `cuts` and the gap tolerances an audit sets · [Mixed-Integer Programming](https://developers.google.com/optimization/mip) (OR-Tools guide) · [Vielma, Mixed Integer Linear Programming Formulation Techniques](https://juan-pablo-vielma.github.io/publications/Mixed-Integer-Linear-Programming-Formulation-Techniques.pdf), introduction and section 2.2: why the effect of a formulation on a state-of-the-art solver is hard to predict, and why a quick computational test of several formulations is the practical answer.
Challenges

items: Run the audit on GridCap small with hard crew rows (`crews=True`). Predict which levers find something, then check against lesson 6.7.2's outputs.
Solve both medium models with `presolve=mathopt.Emphasis.OFF`. Predict whether their root bounds move apart, and whether the reformulated model's node count falls below the inherited one's.
Generate GridCap medium with two other seeds and repeat `case_solve.py`. Before running, decide what result would change the advice in the last rule.

blocks.text: Design Note: Write the Audit as a Program

Every number in this lesson came from two short programs that build each variant of the model from one builder with switches (`fronts=`, `precedence=`). That makes the audit repeatable: when the data change, or the solver is upgraded, the same programs say whether the advice still holds. An audit that lives in a slide deck says what was true once.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**case_audit.py.** Size, LP bound and root bound for each step, the inherited LP's fractional values, and the three levers (*Measure Before You Reformulate*, *The LP Point Shows Where a Formulation Is Weak*, *Try Each Lever*). *Try:* Set `FEE_SHARE` to 0.01 in `strong_model.py`. Predict how far the inherited LP bound falls.
